reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: The historical LEOPARD acronym summarises the features: Lentigines, ECG conduction abnormalities, Ocular hypertelorism, Pulmonary stenosis, Abnormal genitalia, Retarded growth and Deafness
Multiple small dark lentigines appear over the face, neck and trunk during childhood and increase with age, alongside larger cafe-au-lait-like macules
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the most important cardiac lesion and a major determinant of outcome, often accompanied by pulmonary valve stenosis and ECG conduction changes
Most cases arise from specific missense variants in PTPN11 (encoding the phosphatase SHP2), placing it within the RASopathy spectrum alongside Noonan syndrome
Sensorineural hearing loss is common and warrants formal audiological assessment
Facial features overlap with Noonan syndrome: hypertelorism, ptosis, low-set posteriorly rotated ears and a webbed or short neck
Cardiac surveillance with echocardiography and ECG is central to management given the risk of progressive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia
reference.pathophysiology: This disorder is caused chiefly by missense variants in PTPN11 that alter the SHP2 protein tyrosine phosphatase; unlike the activating variants of classic Noonan syndrome, several of these are catalytically impairing yet still dysregulate RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT signalling. The abnormal signalling disturbs cardiac development and myocardial growth, producing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and valvar pulmonary stenosis, while effects on melanocytes generate the progressive lentigines. The same pathway disturbances underlie the craniofacial, auditory and growth features shared with the wider RASopathy family.
additionalInvestigations: RASopathy gene panel including PTPN11, RAF1 and BRAF
Echocardiography to detect hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and pulmonary stenosis
12-lead ECG and Holter monitoring for conduction and rhythm abnormalities
Formal audiometry for sensorineural hearing loss
Growth monitoring and endocrine review where indicated
Dermatological documentation and mapping of lentigines
redFlags: Progressive left ventricular outflow obstruction or symptomatic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Ventricular arrhythmia, syncope or family history of sudden cardiac death
Severe or progressive sensorineural hearing loss affecting speech development
reference.prognosis: Outlook is largely governed by the cardiac phenotype; many patients do well with monitoring, but severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy carries a risk of heart failure and sudden death, so lifelong cardiology follow-up is essential.
pitfalls: Attributing the cafe-au-lait macules to neurofibromatosis and missing the cardiac and pigmentary pattern
Underestimating the risk of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which can progress even when early echocardiography is normal
Failing to arrange hearing assessment, delaying support for sensorineural deafness
Assuming the PTPN11 variants behave like classic Noonan activating variants when counselling

management: Prioritise cardiac care for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — the major determinant of outcome — with monitoring and pharmacological therapy such as beta-blockers, alongside management of any pulmonary valve stenosis
Perform electrocardiography and Holter monitoring for conduction abnormalities and arrhythmia, with lifelong cardiology follow-up given the risk of sudden death
Assess hearing formally with audiometry and provide amplification for sensorineural hearing loss
Document and map the lentigines dermatologically, reassuring that they are cosmetic while distinguishing them from concerning pigmented lesions
Monitor growth and arrange endocrine review where short stature warrants it
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant PTPN11-associated RASopathy, with assessment of relatives
Coordinate lifelong multidisciplinary follow-up across cardiology, audiology, clinical genetics and dermatology
